messages.author: b393c281bb78608e
messages.subject: Inquiry regarding data merging
parts:
Dear all,

National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey released the physical activity monitor raw data of 2011-2014 in October, 2022. It is .csv format derived from ActiGraph GT3X+.

Here is the website: https://wwwn.cdc.gov/Nchs/Nhanes/2011-2012/PAX80_G.htm

In NHANES 2011-2012 cycle, accelerometry data is available for 6,917 participants 6 years and older. The current release (PAX80_G) consists of 6,917 zipped archive files – one for each participant. Due to the very large quantity of the data, these files are stored at the CDC File Transfer Protocol (FTP) Server. The number such as “62161” in the first picture is the number of one participant.

Each participant may have up to 194 hours of accelerometer measurement records. I downloaded the first zipped archive files, which contains the accelerometry information of one participant called “62161”. After the decompression, there are many hourly accelerometer files and one log file aiming to quality control. Each file contains the hourly accelerometry information of this participant. I hope to merge all .csv file as shown in the second picture into one .csv file every time I use GGIR to cope with accelerometry data. I hope to know whether GGIR has this function to merge the information from all .csv file into one .csv file, or whether GGIR can cope with hourly accelerometry information and have the output?


Kind Regards,

Jane.

messages.author: 05de4f382b390d3d
messages.subject: Re: Inquiry regarding data merging
parts:
Hi Jane,

I have not tried this function with NHANES data, but GGIR recently implemented the function to append accelerometer files with the same ID (the definition of idloc is important for this to work). Please see the argument maxRecordingInterval to try this out.

Best,
Jairo

My approach when working with the 2011-2014 NHANES data was to first merge all .csv files per participant (parallelised on a cluster) and then continue processing the combined .csv files with GGIR. messages.subject: Fw: [GGIR] Re: Inquiry regarding data merging
parts:
Hi Fabian, 
Thank you very much for your reply! Actually, now I am trying to merge all .csv files as you mentioned. Firstly, I delete the first file named “logs” regarding quality control using R. Secondly, I use the Command Prompt of Windows to merge all .csv files into one. And then use GGIR function to cope with the raw data of each participant.

However, we all know that there are more than 14,000 participants having raw accelerometry data from 2011 to 2014. And I cannot deal with so much data by myself. I will rent the server. So I need a more simple and automated approach to merge data aiming to save time. The steps I mentioned above are sophisticated because every time I need to rename the merged file of this participant and only in this way can GGIR identify the participant’s id. Such operations will add time for processing data. So I am asking for your help. Can you tell me more details about parallelised on a cluster?

Thank you again for sharing your ideas with me! Looking forward to your reply!

Kind Regards,
Jane.

messages.author: 074c5125059cac06
messages.subject: Re: Fw: [GGIR] Re: Inquiry regarding data merging
parts:
My workflow follows a similar approach to Fabian's, with the following steps:

1. Download all tar.bz2 files.
2. Extract the .bz2 and .tar files into individual folders.
3. Delete the log file. Use xargs and awk to append all CSV files into a single CSV per folder, ensuring the output file (named using the SEQN) contains only one header row.
4. Run the GGIR analysis on the merged CSV using read.myacc.csv.

I am running this using a Snakemake workflow on a cluster with 128GB of RAM and 8 CPU cores, achieving an average processing time of approximately 1 minute per SEQN.

Xiaoyu

Best,
Dave

I have done the same thing, and your code looks correct. However, you need more memory (at least 64 GB). Additionally, you need to add rmc.dynamic_range = 6; otherwise, the clipping score in GGIR will always be exactly 0.  

Xiaoyu

My workflow follows a similar approach to Fabian's, with the following steps:

1. Download all tar.bz2 files.
2. Extract the .bz2 and .tar files into individual folders.
3. Delete the log file. Use xargs and awk to append all CSV files into a single CSV per folder, ensuring the output file (named using the SEQN) contains only one header row.
4. Run the GGIR analysis on the merged CSV using read.myacc.csv.

I am running this using a Snakemake workflow on a cluster with 128GB of RAM and 8 CPU cores, achieving an average processing time of approximately 1 minute per SEQN.
